summary.text: Maximum likelihood estimation estimates the parameters of an assumed probability distribution from observed data.
It does this by maximizing a likelihood function, so that under the assumed model the observed data is most probable.
Its logic is intuitive and flexible, and the method has become a dominant means of statistical inference.

facts.label: Goal
facts.value: Estimate parameters of an assumed distribution from observed data

facts.label: The estimate
facts.value: The point in parameter space that maximizes the likelihood function

facts.label: Consistency
facts.value: The sequence of estimates converges in probability to the true value

facts.label: Regression link
facts.value: Ordinary least squares maximizes likelihood when errors are normal with equal variance

items.prompt: A statistician assumes some data came from a certain type of distribution with unknown settings. How does maximum likelihood choose the settings?

options.label: It picks the settings closest to the sample median
It picks the settings under which the observed data is most probable
It picks the settings that make the next value certain
It picks the settings most earlier studies agreed on

items.explain: The method maximizes a likelihood function so that, under the assumed model, the observed data is most probable.

items.prompt: As more data comes in, a sequence of maximum likelihood estimates settles ever closer to the value being estimated. What does this say about the estimator?

options.label: The estimates converge in probability to the true value
Every single estimate equals the true value exactly
The estimate is identical on every sample drawn
The estimator needs no model of the data at all

items.explain: Consistency means the sequence of maximum likelihood estimates converges in probability to the value being estimated.

items.prompt: Statisticians joke that all models are wrong. What does that imply for the consistency of maximum likelihood in real applications?

options.label: It is guaranteed whenever there is plenty of data
It means the method should never be used at all
True consistency doesn't occur in practice, though it is still desirable
It holds only when the sample is very small

items.explain: Since models are idealized, true consistency does not occur in practical applications, but it is still considered a desirable property for an estimator.

items.prompt: With a very large sample, how does the maximum likelihood estimator compare with other consistent estimators in average squared error?

options.label: It is usually worse, because it assumes a model
It does no better than a plain guess
Other estimators do better as the sample grows
No consistent estimator has lower asymptotic error

items.explain: It achieves the Cramér-Rao lower bound as the sample size grows, so no consistent estimator has lower asymptotic mean squared error.

items.prompt: Two analysts run maximum likelihood on the same data but assume different kinds of distribution. What should we expect?

options.label: They can get different estimates, since the data is judged most probable under each assumed model
They get identical estimates, because the data they used is the same data
Neither can get any estimate unless a prior study exists first
Whoever assumed the more complicated model always wins out

items.explain: The estimate makes the data most probable under the assumed statistical model, so changing the assumed model can change the answer.

items.prompt: A line-fitting method called ordinary least squares is run on data. Under what assumption does it also maximize the likelihood?

options.label: That the data points are all equally spaced
That the line must pass through the origin
That the random errors are normal with the same variance
That the sample contains exactly two groups

items.explain: For a linear regression model, the ordinary least squares estimator maximizes the likelihood when the random errors are assumed to have normal distributions with the same variance.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Maximum likelihood estimation, or MLE, is a way to estimate the parameters of a probability distribution you have assumed, using data you have already observed. The tool at its heart is the likelihood function. You push that function as high as it will go, which picks out the parameter values under which your observed data would be most probable. The point where the function peaks is called the maximum likelihood estimate.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The reasoning behind MLE is easy to follow and bends to fit many problems. That combination has made it a dominant way of doing statistical inference. It also sits comfortably in two different viewpoints. Seen from Bayesian inference, MLE is generally the same as maximum a posteriori estimation when the prior distribution is uniform over the region you care about. Seen from frequentist inference, it is a special case of an extremum estimator, where the quantity being maximized is the likelihood.

paragraphs.heading: How the peak is found
paragraphs.text: If the likelihood function is differentiable, you can use the derivative test for finding a maximum. In some cases the resulting first-order conditions can be solved analytically. Linear regression is one such case: when the random errors are assumed to be normal with equal variance, the ordinary least squares estimator is exactly the one that maximizes the likelihood. It helps that most common distributions, the exponential family among them, are logarithmically concave.

paragraphs.heading: Useful properties
paragraphs.text: MLE has several useful properties. Consistency means the sequence of estimates converges in probability to the value being estimated. Equivariance means that if you apply a one-to-one transform g to the parameter θ, the estimate for g(θ) is simply g applied to the original estimate θ̂. Efficiency means that, as the sample size tends to infinity, MLE reaches the Cramér–Rao lower bound, so no consistent estimator has lower asymptotic mean squared error. That also implies MLE has asymptotic normality.

paragraphs.heading: All models are wrong
paragraphs.text: There is a catch in that first property. In real applications, data are never produced by the model itself; the model is an often idealized picture of whatever process produced them. Statisticians like to say that all models are wrong. So true consistency never happens in practice, yet it is still widely treated as a property worth having.

paragraphs.heading: When parameters must obey rules
paragraphs.text: Sometimes the parameters are not free and must satisfy a constraint written h(θ) = 0, so the task becomes finding the largest likelihood that respects it. For a multivariate normal distribution, for instance, Σ, the covariance matrix, has to be positive-definite. One trick is to write Σ = Γ^T Γ, with Γ a real matrix that is upper triangular, which builds the rule into the parameters. Another approach uses Lagrange multipliers, and if a constraint is not binding at the maximum, its multipliers should come out as zero. That fact gives a way to test whether the constraint is valid, known as the Lagrange multiplier test.
